newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says Hong Kong deal promotes its WTO entry.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says Hong Kong deal promotes its WTO entry.

text.p: Taiwan said on Wednesday it had reached an initial agreement with Hong Kong that, if ratified, removes any Hong Kong objections to the island's membership in the World Trade Organisation.
Taiwan's economics ministry said negotiators from Taipei and Hong Kong signed the preliminary pact in Tokyo late on Tuesday after a sixth round of bilateral trade talks.
Taipei, for its part, said it had agreed to further liberalise its textile imports and financial sector.
The agreement was not final and both sides were confirming technical details, the ministry said. "A formal agreement will be signed at a later date," it said.
The talks were the first between Nationalist-ruled Taiwan and Hong Kong since the British colony was handed over to rule by Taiwan's longtime rival, communist China, on July 1.
It was not known whether Hong Kong consulted with its new masters in Beijing before reaching the deal or whether further consultations with the Chinese government were necessary.
Taiwan media said no mainland officials attended the talks.

Beijing has said it would accept Taiwan's membership in the WTO as a "customs territory" but not before China itself gets in as the sole sovereign Chinese member. Hong Kong already has status in the WTO as a customs territory.
Hong Kong trade officials were unavailable for comment.
In 1990, Taiwan applied to join the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, as a customs territory under the name of Chinese Taipei.
Under WTO accession rules, members are allowed to seek bilateral talks with applicants to negotiate what they regard as acceptable trade relations, including market access.
An agreement reached in these bilateral talks implies that the WTO member, for its part, has no objections to the applicant's bid to join.

Including Hong Kong, Taiwan has completed negotiations with all but six of the 26 WTO members that sought such talks. It still lacks agreements with the United States, the European Union, Canada, Singapore, Switzerland and Argentina.

Beijing has vowed to let Hong Kong largely run itself with a large degree of autonomy and said there should be no change in Taiwan's huge business ties with Hong Kong, which serves as a gateway for large Taiwan investment flows into China.
Beijing nonetheless requires that Hong Kong-Taiwan contacts be vetted by the communist government, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a 1949 civil war split.
Taipei said that in the talks with Hong Kong it stood firm in its determination to regulate the operations of businesses funded or controlled by interests in mainland China.
Trade officials stressed that it was communist China proper, not the new Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, that was targetted by Taiwan's investment and trade controls.
"We explained to the Hong Kong side about the rules that restrict mainland funds. They are not discriminating against Hong Kong," the economic ministry said in a statement.
Beijing has subjected Taiwan to a tight diplomatic embargo in hopes of forcing it under communist sovereignty.

Worried that China will use economic leverage in Hong Kong to squeeze the island, Taiwan carefully vets all firms suspected of having mainland backing and subjects those whose mainland ownership exceeds 20 percent to tough scrutiny.
Taipei maintains a right to veto such projects.

The Taiwan ministry said that under the deal, Taipei would grant initial negotiation rights to Hong Kong for more than 200 textile and garment products, meaning that Taipei must consult with Hong Kong before it can raise tariffs on those products.
Taipei said it agreed to cut a range of import tariffs on those products. The ministry declined to give details.
Taiwan said it also agreed to unspecified liberalisations in its banking, insurance and financial sectors.
